title: A launch post that is not a press release
metaTitle: A launch page that shows the change
excerpt: A launch page should say what changed for the user, show it, and give one next action. Internal milestones belong in a memo, not on the page.
alt: A pale room with an arched opening onto a dark sofa, a low table, and a glass vase of dried stems, a scene you can understand at a glance.
caption: A room you can read without a tour. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs on a product launch page?
faqs.answer: The change for the user, a view of the real product, and one next action that works today. Say the limit if people will otherwise hit it in front of their own customer. Internal milestones, code names, and a list of thanks belong in a company note.

faqs.question: What should the launch page title say?
faqs.answer: It should state the new ability, not only the word launch or a version number. The share preview should carry the same fact, because many people will only read that line. If you cannot write a specific title, the launch is not ready.

faqs.question: Should a launch page stay up afterward?
faqs.answer: Yes. People will keep arriving from old links, and the page should still explain that change. Edit it when support questions show a missing line. Give the next change its own address rather than stacking a second announcement on the first URL.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A product launch page should say what changed for the user, show that change, and give one next action. A list of internal milestones is a memo to the team. It can live in the company chat. The page is for the person who was not in the room and needs to know whether their work got easier.

Write the page the way you would explain the change to a customer on a call. Then delete the parts that only matter to the team that shipped it. The reader is deciding whether to try the change, not whether to applaud the sprint.

## What changed for them

Start with the task that is different today. "You can send the agreement from the same screen as the draft" is a change. "We are thrilled to announce our biggest release" is a mood. The mood can be one clause. The change is the page.

Name the person. If the change is for clinic managers, say clinic managers. If it is for anyone, you may not have a change yet. You may have a feature. A feature becomes a launch when a specific person can do a specific thing they could not do last week.

Say the before in a line, if the before is widely true. "Previously this was a download, a rename, and an email." Then the after. People recognize themselves in the before. They do not recognize themselves in your sprint number.

Leave the funding, the headcount, and the months of effort off the first screen. Those are costs you paid. The reader is deciding whether to try the thing. Effort is not a feature. If the effort produced a real capability, show the capability.

[Google's title-link guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) says the title should describe the page. "Launch," "Update," and "Announcing v2" do not describe a change. A title that states the new ability will be the line people forward. Write that title first, and let the headline match it. If the headline cannot be specific, the launch is not ready to publish. You are still announcing that you worked.

## Show it

A launch that does not show the change asks for trust you have not earned on the page. Show the screen, the object, or the before and after. Use the real product. A mock with fake data named "Acme" tells a careful reader that the feature is a sketch.

Crop to the change. A full desktop with forty panels hides the thing you shipped. One view, with the new control visible, beats a tour of the entire app. If there are two steps, show two views and number them. If the change is a speed or a result, show the result in a way that is true. Do not invent a percentage. If you have a measured one from your own product, label what it measures and the period. If you do not, describe the change in plain steps and skip the chart.

Motion can show a flow when the flow is the change. Keep it short, and keep a still frame for the person who will not watch. The still frame should contain the point. Autoplay with sound is a bad launch. The person is often in a tab at work.

Captions should say what the reader is seeing. "The new send step, on the draft" is a caption. "Beautiful new UI" is a compliment you paid yourself. Alt text should match the frame, for the same reason the [W3C accessibility guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) treat images that carry information as content that needs a text alternative. The screenshot is evidence. The alternative should state the evidence.

If the product is private, show only what you can. A blurred full interface shows nothing. A described step, plus a single real fragment you are allowed to show, is more honest. Do not illustrate the launch with a stock scene of a team high-fiving. That photograph is about you. The page is about them.

## One next action

The action matches the change. Try the feature, if they already have an account. Start a trial, if that is true. Book a call, if the change is something you still roll out with help. Read the short guide, if the change needs a step they will miss.

Pick one. A launch page with "start free," "talk to sales," "read the docs," and "join the community" is a directory. The reader came to understand a change. Give them the door that fits that change. The other doors can be text links in a quiet line.

Make the action possible today. A button that opens a waitlist for a feature you said is live is a contradiction. If it is live for some accounts, say which ones. "Available now on the team plan" is a fact. "Available now" when it is not is how launches become support tickets.

If the action is a call, use the same sentence on the button that you use in the email you will send. The page, the mail, and the in-app notice should agree. Disagreement looks like three companies.

Log in should not be required to understand the change. It may be required to use it. The explanation is public. The product can be gated. People forward launch pages to colleagues who do not have accounts yet. Those colleagues are part of the decision.

## Milestones that belong in the memo

Keep a separate note for the company. Ship date, who did the work, what you cut, what you will watch this week. That note is useful and it is not the launch. The public page should not be that note with a hero image.

These lines belong in the memo:

- The internal code name.
- The number of commits, the late nights, the all-hands.
- Thanks to every department, in a list.
- The roadmap of what you might build next, in any detail a competitor or a confused customer will treat as a promise.
- Apologies for the delay, unless the delay itself harmed users and you owe them a plain account of what is fixed.

A short thanks to the customers who tested the change is public-appropriate when it is specific and true. "Thanks to the clinics that tried the send step in March" is enough. A paragraph about your journey is the memo again.

Version numbers can be on the page if your users use them. Many do not. Lead with the ability. Put the version in a quiet line for the people who file bugs.

## The shape of the page

A single page is the right shape for one change. Title, the change, the picture, the action. A short second section for who it is for, if that is not obvious. A third for the limit: what it does not do yet, if the limit will otherwise become a support burden.

Limits build more trust than a universal claim. "This sends the agreement. It does not yet store the signed file in your archive" is a launch a professional can use. They will plan around the limit. If you hide it, they will discover it in front of their customer.

The page should be fast on a phone. A launch will be opened from a chat app. Compress the picture. Do not wrap the page in a marketing shell that loads a second navigation, a chat widget, and a banner about a different campaign. The campaign is this change.

Set the title, the share description, and the first sentence to the same fact. When the link is pasted, the preview should say the change. If the preview says the company slogan, you wasted the only line many people will read.

Publish when the action works. A launch URL that 404s for an hour is a self-inflicted story. Check the form, the feature flag, and the screenshot one last time on a phone that is not logged in as an admin. Admin states lie. They show buttons ordinary accounts do not have.

## The day after

Read the support mail and the replies. The questions you get are the lines the page failed to say. Add those lines. A launch page can be edited. Treating it as a frozen announcement is how a small confusion becomes the public definition of the feature.

Do not immediately stack a second campaign on the same URL. If you launch again next month, give that change its own address, and let this one remain the explanation of this change. People will keep arriving from old links. The page should still be true.

If the launch is also a change in what the company is, the site around the post may now be wrong. Old navigation, old headlines, and old comparisons will contradict the new page. Fixing that is a different job from writing the launch. It is the rewrite after a pivot, and it is next: [rewriting the site after a pivot](/blog/rewriting-the-site-after-a-pivot).

If the change is something you want to show rather than only describe, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min) and bring the before and the after.
